title: Designing a Resilient Multi-Provider AI Gateway on Serverless Runtimes
summary: How 9router and AIDahl pool keys across Gemini, Groq, DeepSeek, OpenAI, and OpenRouter with sub-20ms automatic HTTP 429 failover, per-user AES-GCM vaults, and rate-safe Telegram token streaming.
body:
When you ship an AI assistant to real daily users, the hardest problems rarely come from prompt engineering. They come from upstream reliability: sudden  HTTP 429  rate limits on free or burst tiers, regional latency spikes, provider outages, and the security liability of storing user-supplied API keys.

While building   [9router](https://github.com/mohsen-niksirat/9router TG Bot)   (a multi-provider AI gateway and Telegram Mini App) alongside   [AIDahl](https://github.com/mohsen-niksirat/AIDahl)   (a Bring-Your-Own-Key Telegram research assistant), I needed a routing layer that could treat five distinct model ecosystems (Gemini, Groq, DeepSeek, OpenAI, and OpenRouter) as a single fault-tolerant compute pool.



   Why Single-Provider Wrappers Break Under Real Traffic

Most chat bots wire user input straight to a single SDK endpoint. That works during a solo demo, then fails in three predictable ways once concurrent users arrive:

1.   Token-per-minute (TPM) cliffs:   A single long-context document summary can exhaust a key's per-minute token bucket, blocking every short query behind it.
2.   Heterogeneous payload dialects:   Gemini's native multimodal content parts differ from OpenAI-compatible  chat/completions  schemas, especially around vision attachments and tool calls.
3.   Downstream chat throttling:   Even when Groq streams 400 tokens per second, forwarding every chunk to Telegram's  editMessageText  endpoint triggers a strict flood-wait penalty from Telegram itself.

Solving all three meant separating   key health state  ,   protocol normalization  , and   stream pacing   into independent layers.

   Health-Weighted Key Pooling and 429 Circuit Breaking

Instead of static round-robin rotation, 9router maintains a lightweight health record per key. When an upstream request returns  429 Too Many Requests  or  503 Service Unavailable , the router parses  Retry-After  headers (falling back to an exponential cooldown with random jitter) and immediately retries the request against the next healthy credential or fallback provider.

title: PBKDF2 Iteration Counts for Offline Browser Vaults
summary: In API Key Manager, deriving a 256-bit AES-GCM key via WebCrypto PBKDF2-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations takes ~190ms on modern laptops and ~420ms on mid-range Android phones: fast enough for a single unlock prompt while raising brute-force cost substantially without external WASM bundles.

title: Preventing Punctuation Flip in Bilingual RTL Technical Prose
summary: Inline code spans like `HTTP 429` or `O(N log N)` inside Persian paragraphs scramble parentheses unless styled with `unicode-bidi: isolate` and `direction: ltr`. Applying isolation at the base `code` selector fixes bidirectional cursor movement and copy-paste order across Ravaan and this journal.

title: Silence Thresholds in Spoken English Tutoring
summary: Standard 500ms voice-activity cutoffs interrupt non-native speakers mid-thought while searching for vocabulary. Extending end-of-turn silence tolerance to 1,250ms in SpeakAI Coach produced far more accurate 6-axis IELTS fluency and lexical resource scoring.

title: Flat Float32Array Weights for In-Browser Neuroevolution
summary: In Biosphera, representing each digital organism's tiny neural network as a contiguous `Float32Array` slice rather than nested JS arrays cut crossover/mutation garbage collection pauses to near zero at 60 FPS.

title: Lookahead Scheduling with AudioContext.currentTime
summary: JavaScript `setInterval` drifts by 10–40ms whenever the main thread paints. In Tonora, scheduling Web Audio oscillator envelopes 100ms ahead against hardware `audioCtx.currentTime` keeps chord playback rhythmically tight even on mobile browsers.
